title: Roles of Various Groups in Elderly Care

headings.title: Introduction to Gerontological Care Teams
headings.content: Gerontological care teams are multidisciplinary groups dedicated to meeting the complex, multifaceted health needs of older adults. As the global and Nigerian population ages, the demand for specialized care that goes beyond traditional acute medical treatment increases. Gerontological care recognizes that elderly patients often suffer from multiple chronic illnesses, functional impairments, and psychosocial challenges simultaneously. Consequently, relying on a single healthcare provider is insufficient. A comprehensive care team brings together various medical, nursing, therapeutic, and social support professionals to optimize the health-related quality of life for seniors. For nursing students in Nigeria, understanding this collaborative framework is essential because you will frequently act as the central coordinator among these diverse professionals. The ultimate goal of the gerontological care team is to promote healthy aging, prevent functional decline, manage chronic conditions effectively, and ensure dignity and comfort at every stage of the older adult's life journey. By working cohesively, team members can address physical symptoms while simultaneously tending to the emotional, social, and environmental determinants of health that profoundly impact elderly populations.

headings.title: Primary Roles of Registered Nurses and Nursing Assistants
headings.content: Registered Nurses (RNs) and Nursing Assistants (NAs) form the backbone of daily elderly care in hospitals, clinics, and long-term care facilities. Registered Nurses hold a pivotal leadership and clinical role, conducting comprehensive health assessments, formulating nursing care plans, administering medications, monitoring for adverse drug reactions, and educating both patients and their families. RNs are skilled at identifying subtle changes in an older adult's baseline health, which can indicate the onset of complications such as delirium, sepsis, or quiet heart failures. Meanwhile, Nursing Assistants provide crucial direct patient care under the supervision of RNs. They assist elderly individuals with activities of daily living (ADLs) such as bathing, dressing, grooming, feeding, and safe ambulation. NAs often spend the most direct time with patients, making them exceptionally well-positioned to report changes in skin integrity, mood, or appetite back to the nursing staff. Together, RNs and NAs ensure that care is continuous, compassionate, and tailored to the unique vulnerabilities of the geriatric patient. In the Nigerian healthcare context, where family members often participate heavily in bedside care, professional nurses also have the critical duty of guiding and supervising informal caregivers to maintain high standards of clinical safety.

headings.title: Contributions of Physicians and Geriatricians
headings.content: Physicians and specialized geriatricians drive the medical diagnosis, medical treatment regimens, and overall clinical management of older adult patients. A general practitioner manages routine health issues, but a geriatrician has specialized training in diagnosing and treating the unique, overlapping health conditions common in old age, such as dementia, osteoporosis, multiple chronic comorbidities, and polypharmacy. Physicians evaluate complex symptoms, order and interpret diagnostic investigations, prescribe targeted medical therapies, and determine the appropriateness of surgical or invasive interventions. In geriatric medicine, a crucial aspect of the physician's role is managing 'polypharmacy'—the concurrent use of multiple medications—by regularly reviewing and rationalizing drug prescriptions to prevent adverse drug interactions, falls, and toxicity. Physicians also lead discussions regarding goals of care, advance directives, and palliative interventions when curative options are exhausted. Collaborating closely with nurses and other team members, physicians rely heavily on the continuous monitoring provided by nursing staff to make informed adjustments to medical treatment plans. For student nurses, understanding the physician's diagnostic mindset helps facilitate smoother interprofessional communication and ensures timely execution of medical orders.

headings.title: The Role of Allied Health Professionals: Physiotherapy, Occupational Therapy, and Pharmacy
headings.content: Allied health professionals—specifically physiotherapists, occupational therapists, and clinical pharmacists—play indispensable roles in maintaining and restoring the functional independence of older adults. Physiotherapists focus on mobility, muscle strength, balance, and gait training, which are critical for preventing devastating falls and managing joint or muscular pain associated with arthritis or stroke recovery. Occupational therapists (OTs) evaluate an older adult's ability to perform meaningful daily activities and recommend environmental modifications, adaptive equipment, and techniques to maximize independence in self-care, cooking, and household management. Clinical pharmacists are medication experts who collaborate with physicians and nurses to screen for drug-drug interactions, optimize dosing regimens based on renal and hepatic clearance in aging bodies, and educate patients on correct drug administration. For example, a pharmacist can identify if an older adult is experiencing confusion due to an anticholinergic medication burden. When these allied health professionals work alongside nursing staff, care becomes truly comprehensive, addressing both internal pharmacological safety and external physical functioning. Student nurses must learn to recognize when a referral to an allied health professional is necessary to improve a patient's overall prognosis and quality of life.

headings.title: Social Workers and Case Managers in Elderly Support
headings.content: Social workers and case managers serve as vital links between the older adult, their family, and the broader health and social welfare systems. Social workers assess the psychosocial, emotional, and financial needs of seniors and their families. They provide counseling, assist with navigating complex healthcare bureaucracy, and connect families with community resources, government assistance programs, and long-term placement options when home care is no longer feasible. Case managers coordinate the entire continuum of care, ensuring that transitions—such as moving from a hospital acute care ward back to the home or a rehabilitation center—are safe, organized, and seamless. They monitor resource utilization, advocate for patient rights, and prevent gaps in service delivery that frequently lead to preventable hospital readmissions. In Nigeria, where formal long-term care facilities are limited and social security safety nets can be fragile, social workers and case managers often play an invaluable advocacy role. They help families mobilize informal networks, access charitable health initiatives, and cope with the immense emotional and financial burden of caring for an aging relative with chronic disabling conditions like dementia.

headings.title: Family Caregivers and Informal Support Systems
headings.content: Family caregivers and informal support systems are the bedrock of elderly care, particularly in Nigeria and many other developing nations where cultural norms emphasize filial piety and community-based living. Informal caregivers—including spouses, adult children, and extended family members—provide the vast majority of day-to-day physical, emotional, and financial support that keeps older adults in their homes and communities. They assist with feeding, hygiene, medication reminders, transportation to clinics, and emotional companionship. However, providing continuous care can lead to severe 'caregiver burnout,' characterized by physical exhaustion, emotional stress, anxiety, and depression. Professional nurses have a vital responsibility to assess not only the patient but also the well-being of the family caregiver. This involves offering education on proper transfer techniques, providing emotional reassurance, connecting them with respite care resources, and validating their hard work. Recognizing informal caregivers as true partners in the healthcare team ensures that the care plan remains realistic, culturally appropriate, and sustainable over the long term.

headings.title: Community-Based Organizations and Support Groups
headings.content: Community-based organizations (CBOs), faith-based institutions, and support groups form an essential outer layer of support for older adults and their families. In many Nigerian communities, churches, mosques, and local age-grade or neighborhood associations provide vital social interaction, spiritual sustenance, financial aid, and volunteer-based home visits for isolated seniors. Support groups specifically tailored for caregivers or individuals with chronic illnesses like dementia offer safe spaces for sharing coping strategies, reducing social isolation, and receiving peer encouragement. Additionally, community health clinics organize wellness outreach programs, blood pressure screenings, and health education seminars tailored to the geriatric population. For student nurses, engaging with these community resources allows for holistic nursing care that extends far beyond hospital walls. By referring patients and families to local CBOs and support groups, nurses help build a sustainable safety net that promotes active aging, combats loneliness, and enhances overall community resilience against health disparities in old age.

headings.title: Interprofessional Collaboration and Communication in Geriatric Care
headings.content: Interprofessional collaboration and effective communication are the cornerstones of safe, high-quality geriatric care. Because older adults frequently transition between various health states and care settings, fragmented communication between doctors, nurses, therapists, social workers, and family members can lead to medical errors, adverse drug events, and patient harm. Interprofessional collaboration means that healthcare providers actively consult, respect, and coordinate with one another, viewing each discipline's expertise as complementary rather than isolated. Tools such as structured handoff communication (e.g., SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation), shared electronic or paper health records, and regular multidisciplinary team meetings facilitate this seamless exchange of information. For nursing students, mastering interprofessional communication is paramount. As nurses are often present at the center of patient care operations, you will frequently facilitate information flow, advocate for the patient's needs during team conferences, and ensure that the unified care plan is understood and executed by everyone involved, including the family.
